The underlying problem it addresses is easy to understand. Recently, the culture of writing

with tools like Claude Code and Cursor has spread significantly, but there has been almost no way to verify if the written skills are working as intended or if the quality is maintained when switching models.
waza standardizes this "evaluation" process. You write evaluation tasks in YAML, run them repeatedly, and score whether the skills are functioning as expected.
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/waza/main/install.sh | bash

The grading is handled by a grader (validator), and there are roughly four types: 'code' which looks at structures like the presence of function definitions, 'text' which checks for expected keywords using regular expressions, 'behavior' which monitors token limits or tool call counts, and 'llm-judge' which uses another LLM as a judge.
Since you can assign a 'weight' to each, it's quite thoughtful that you can declaratively write a scoring policy like 'behavior is a reference value, prioritize llm-judge'.

There are two executors for execution mode: 'mock', which returns deterministic fake responses without needing an API key, and 'copilot-sdk', which actually hits the model. A two-stage approach is recommended: running fast with mock during the design phase or PRs, and using copilot-sdk for production evaluation.
The workflow itself is surprisingly simple, and you can go through it in 5 minutes.

The practical example I picked up from an application article here was quite suggestive. The subject is a skill that creates commit messages in Conventional Commits format, and the verification involves taking scores with waza every time it is revised.

For the initial minimal configuration, gpt-5.4 scored 0.88 and claude-opus-4.6 also scored 0.88. When I listed 5 mandatory elements saying 'be more careful', gpt-5.4 compressed the subject into one line and it
In other words, increasing instructions can cause compression or contradictions depending on the model.

The good points are clear, and above all, it has a strong power to deny the 'intention to improve'. Like the example earlier, it can spot in one go that a revision you thought was a step forward is actually a regression.

On the other hand, there are quite a few challenges, such as the authentication hurdle being quite high when running copilot-sdk on CI. The `skill_invocation` grader that detects skill activation is still hard to call practical in the current version.
llm-judge provides accuracy, but since costs balloon if you run it on every PR, a nightly batch seems to be the realistic solution.
The fact that a skill optimized for testing fails in production is the exact same structure as code testing, which I found very insightful.
